extra.message: Sensitive data exposure via unauthenticated debug endpoint — Any unauthenticated attacker can dump all usernames and plaintext passwords, leading to full account takeover of every user. [verified: debug() calls get_all_users_debug() and is wired to an endpoint with no token_validator call, exposing plaintext passwords/emails/admin flags to anyone.]

Plaintext password storage and user/password enumeration on login — Attacker can enumerate valid usernames via distinct error messages, and a DB compromise (e.g. via the SQLi above) directly exposes usable plaintext credentials. [verified: Password comparison is plain '==' against user.password with no hashing anywhere in User model/login path, and the enumeration branch is present as in finding 3.]

Broken Object Level Authorization allows overwriting another user's password — Any authenticated attacker can take over any other account by setting its password, since only an auth token for *some* user is required, not ownership of the target account. [verified: update_password uses the path username, not resp['sub'], to select the target user and overwrites its password when vuln is true, with no ownership check.]

Broken authorization allows overwriting arbitrary user's password — Any authenticated (even low-privilege) user can take over any other account, including admin, by resetting its password. [verified: Same root cause as idx 0: update_password trusts the path-supplied username instead of the authenticated resp['sub'].]

Hardcoded weak JWT secret key — An attacker who guesses or discovers the trivial secret 'random' can forge valid JWTs for any username, achieving full authentication bypass and impersonation of any user including admins. [verified: config.py:13 hardcodes SECRET_KEY='random', used as HMAC key for JWT signing/verification, allowing forgery of tokens for any user.]

Hardcoded/weak JWT and Flask SECRET_KEY — Attacker forges arbitrary JWT auth tokens (e.g. for an admin user) and fully bypasses authentication/authorization [verified: Same hardcoded 'random' secret at config.py:13 is used by jwt.encode/decode in user_model.py, enabling full auth bypass via forged tokens.]

Debug endpoint exposes all user credentials without authentication — Any unauthenticated attacker can dump every user's plaintext password, email, and admin status. [verified: debug() in api_views/users.py calls User.get_all_users_debug()/json_debug() with no token_validator or any auth check, exposing plaintext passwords and admin flags.]

SQL Injection in get_user via f-string query — Attacker can inject SQL through the username in GET /users/v1/{username} to exfiltrate arbitrary data (e.g. all users/passwords) or manipulate the query, potentially achieving full DB read/write. [verified: username flows unsanitized from get_by_username (no auth) into an f-string SQL query executed via db.session.execute(text(...)).]

Broken Object Level Authorization on book retrieval — Any authenticated user can read any other user's private book secret_content by guessing/enumerating book titles. [verified: In vuln mode, get_by_title queries Book solely by book_title with no ownership filter against resp['sub'], directly exposing secret_content and owner to any authenticated user.]

IDOR / BOLA on book secret_content — Any authenticated user can read any other user's private book secret_content by guessing/enumerating book titles. [verified: Same code path confirmed: Book.query.filter_by(book_title=...).first() in the vuln branch lacks any user/ownership scoping, so any authenticated caller can read another user's secret_content by enumerating titles.]

Mass assignment / privilege escalation via admin field at registration — Anonymous attacker can register an account with admin=true, granting themselves administrative privileges (e.g. ability to delete other users). [verified: register_user directly honors request_data['admin'] with no authorization check when vuln is true, letting any anonymous registrant set admin=true.]

Flask debug mode enabled in production entrypoint — If an unhandled exception surfaces the Werkzeug interactive debugger, an unauthenticated attacker can execute arbitrary Python code on the server, fully compromising it [verified: Same line confirms debug=True is hardcoded and reachable at startup, exposing the Werkzeug console on any unhandled exception.]

Mass assignment of admin flag at registration — A newly registered account can self-elevate to admin privileges, gaining access to admin-only functions such as delete_user. [verified: register_user() sets admin=True from request body when vuln flag is set, with no restriction on who can do this (public endpoint).]

Missing authentication on database reset endpoint — Any anonymous user can wipe and reset the entire users/books database at will, causing data loss/denial of service. [verified: populate_db() calls db.drop_all()/create_all() with no auth decorator or security scheme in openapi3.yml's /createdb path, so any anonymous caller can wipe and reset the database.]

Unauthenticated user profile lookup — Any unauthenticated attacker can enumerate and retrieve email/username data for arbitrary accounts by requesting GET /users/v1/{username}. [verified: get_by_username calls User.get_user(username) directly with no token_validator/Authorization check, leaking user data to anonymous callers.]

Missing rate limiting on authentication endpoints — Attacker can brute-force credentials or password resets without throttling, especially damaging combined with the enumeration and plaintext-password issues above. [verified: No rate-limiting decorator, middleware, or lockout counter exists anywhere in login_user/update_password/register_user.]

User/password enumeration on login endpoint — Attacker can enumerate valid usernames and mount targeted credential-stuffing/brute-force attacks with confirmed valid accounts. [verified: login_user returns distinct 'Username does not exist' vs 'Password is not correct' messages under vuln mode with no compensating control.]

Plaintext password storage — Any DB read access (via SQLi finding above, debug endpoint, or DB file access) yields directly usable plaintext credentials for all accounts. [verified: Same plaintext storage/comparison issue confirmed at model level; duplicate of idx 1.]

Plaintext password storage — Any DB compromise (or the debug endpoint above) yields plaintext credentials for every user, enabling credential-stuffing attacks against other services. [verified: User.password stored/compared as plaintext (__init__ sets self.password directly; login_user does request_data.get('password') == user.password), no hashing anywhere.]

Plaintext password storage — Any database compromise, SQLi, or debug-endpoint leak directly exposes usable plaintext credentials for every account. [verified: Duplicate confirmation of plaintext password storage; self.password = password in __init__ with no hashing, and get_user's raw SQL branch also returns password directly.]

Regular Expression Denial of Service in email validation — An authenticated attacker can send a crafted long email string causing catastrophic backtracking, exhausting CPU and blocking the single-threaded Flask worker (DoS). [verified: The nested quantifier regex ((...)+ combined with inner [-.\w]* and [-\w]* groups) is applied to unbounded attacker-controlled email input with no length cap, a plausible catastrophic-backtracking pattern, though Flask threading may limit real DoS impact.]
